title: RingCentral API Limits, Auth and Errors for Developers
summary: The RingCentral API requires authentication and enforces rate limits. Configure access and understand error responses for your integration.
body_markdown:
## Call RingCentral endpoints without code using Activepieces


Without writing code, you can call RingCentral through Activepieces, which is used by teams at MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties.


It holds the RingCentral credentials centrally as a connection, so every flow points at one place instead of each builder keeping keys, and it records every run so you can see where a limit or error was hit.


Open its built-in chat, describe a process that touches your RingCentral connection, and what it publishes is a live flow in your account, the same kind of flow a builder would assemble by hand, with a run trace showing exactly what happened at each step, including the one that returned the limit or error.


That matters most after a renewal check like the one above: you describe the process, and the run trace tells you whether it held.


Read the flow below as the usual shape. A trigger starts the run, a RingCentral piece action does the work the piece supports, and a generic HTTP step calls any RingCentral endpoint the piece lacks.


The takeaway is that one workflow can mix both, so a missing action doesn't force you out of the tool.


### When a no-code RingCentral workflow is enough


Use it when you can describe the process in a sentence: a message arrives, a record is created, a notification goes out.


Ops and support teams are usually the first to build these, and they are the ones to put in front of a template, because a shared flow carries its connection setup and error handling with it and the next team starts from something already tested.


For endpoints the integration doesn't cover, the HTTP step reuses the same RingCentral connection, so the credentials still live in one place.


Check the scopes your app grants against RingCentral's docs on the day you ship, since a step that works in testing can fail under a plan with different permissions. When it fails, open the run trace.


It shows which step returned the error and what RingCentral said, so you fix the cause instead of guessing.


### When to stay with direct API calls


Stay with code when volume is high enough that you need to manage rate limits yourself. The same goes when you need retry logic the flow builder can't express, such as backing off differently per error type or queuing work across many accounts.


Those cases need control over timing and state that a visual step doesn't give you.


Test it with the trace. If you keep opening it to find the same limit being hit, the workflow has outgrown the tool, and a small service you own is the cheaper fix. Until then, describe the process, run it, and read the trace.
